title: Sudden Scale Adaptation and Affinity Matrix PRD (draft)
body:
Overview:
This is a working PRD outlining a lightweight, predictable autoscaling and burst architecture for Dedicated capacity focused on sudden traffic spikes and preserving isolation guarantees. Core idea: treat compute as short-duration 'leases' with an affinity matrix that scores how well a request (customer, model, input shape, SLO) maps to available pool slices. The control plane brokers leases, uses configurable grace windows for preemption, and exposes tenant-level affinity hints to minimize cold-start cost while enabling controlled bursts.

Why this doc exists (problem statement):
- Customers on Dedicated need predictable latency even under unexpected surges, but static overprovisioning is expensive.
- Existing soft-preempt approaches either overreact (wasteful warm pools) or underreact (high tail latency).
- Isolation (noisy neighbor) controls today are coarse: whole-pool throttles or blunt preemption. We need finer-grained adaptivity that respects SLAs and pricing tiers.

High-level goals (what success looks like):
- Maintain 99th percentile latency SLO for tiered customers within 2x cost of baseline steady-state usage during surges.
- Allow controlled bursts of up to 3x committed throughput for short windows (<= 5 minutes) with predictable degradation policies.
- Provide per-tenant affinity scoring so routing favors nodes that reduce cold starts and KV/cache misses.
- Expose clear ops primitives for graceful reclaim (grace periods), forced decommit with checkpoints, and post-burst reconciliations.

Non-goals:
- This doc does not replace long-term capacity market/credit systems; it complements them with a runtime-level lease broker.
- Not aiming to support arbitrary global auto-scale beyond machine-level leases in this phase.

Key concepts introduced:
- Lease: a time-bounded allocation of GPU capacity for a tenant. Leases are short (seconds to minutes) and can be renewed or relinquished.
- Affinity matrix: vector of heuristic scores per tenant/model pairing with host pools. Inputs: model family, average seq length, KV cache hit ratio, recent startup penalty, tenant SLA tier.
- Grace window: a per-lease soft timeout allowing in-flight requests to finish and checkpoint KV state before preemption.
- Burst token: ephemeral credits granted to tenants eligible for burst; tokens decay over time and are reclaimed first.

User stories and scenarios:
- Engineering team (startup tier) experiences a sudden weekly event causing a 5x traffic spike for 3 minutes. Desired: automatic short leases to add capacity without long-term reserved cost; if capacity tight, fall back to degraded token-mode responses (reduced max tokens) rather than dropping connections.
- Enterprise customer (premium tier) requires isolation for steady-state but allows short bursts at a cost. Desired: reserved baseline plus burst tokens with guaranteed grace period and a higher affinity to warm hosts.
- Platform operator needs a transparent list of which leases were preempted and why for post-mortem. Desired: audit stream and reconciler job that reconciles caches and billing.

Product requirements (API & UX):
1) Lease API additions (control plane):
   - POST /leases with fields: tenant_id, requested_gpus, lease_duration_secs, affinity_hint (optional), burst_token_request (bool).
   - Response: lease_id, allocated_hosts[], grace_window_secs, preemption_policy_id.
   - PATCH /leases/{lease_id} to renew or adjust duration.
   - GET /leases?tenant_id=.. for debugging.
   Acceptance criteria: calls succeed with sub-200ms control-plane latency under light load; error codes explain preemption likelihood (low/medium/high).

2) Affinity scoring:
   - Control plane computes an affinity vector per tenant-host pair (0-100). Use a small model combining: historical KV hit delta, recent cold-start latency, model memory footprint, GPU type match.
   - Affinity should be exposed via GET /affinity?tenant=.. returning top N hosts and score reasons (as short tags).
   Acceptance: affinity predictions correlate with reduced cold-start latency in canary tests (>=15% reduction).

3) Graceful reclaim and checkpointing:
   - Lease includes grace_window_secs. Runtime must drain in-flight requests, persist minimal KV checkpoint (if configured), and return HTTP 409 (retry-after) for new requests when reclaiming.
   - Expose per-tenant config: checkpoint_level (none/minimal/full) which affects reclaim timeouts and cost.

4) Burst token lifecycle:
   - Tokens issued based on historical usage, billing tier, and recent surge patterns.
   - Tokens include decay curve; platform may preempt non-token traffic first.

5) Isolation controls and fast-fail modes:
   - Per-host QoS buckets enforced via cgroups and runtime token accounting.
   - Soft-demotion: reduce model max_output_tokens or temperature as a graceful degradation path instead of immediate preemption.

Operational requirements and metrics:
- Metrics to emit: lease_allocations, lease_renew_rate, lease_preempt_count, avg_grace_reclaim_time, affinity_hit_rate (requests hitting host with top-1 affinity), burst_token_consumption_rate, 99p latency by tenant-tier during surges.
- SLOs: control-plane API 95th latency < 250ms; affinity API 95th < 300ms; reclaim end-to-end < configured grace_window + 2s for minimal checkpoint.

Rollout plan (phases):
- Alpha (internal): broker leases for one low-risk host pool; affinity computed from simple heuristics (no ML). Run synthetic surge tests.
- Beta (selected customers): enable burst tokens for opt-in tenants; surface affinity hints to routing; collect cost/latency telemetry.
- GA: fully automatic lease brokering with per-tenant config and UI in Console; billing integration.

Backward compatibility and migration notes:
- Leases are additive; existing reserved capacity paths remain unchanged.
- If a tenant does not opt-in, they receive previous behavior (no short leases, only baseline reservation).

Open questions / risks:
- How to price burst tokens fairly across customers without creating adversarial usage patterns? (billing/behavior research needed)
- Checkpoint overheads for large KV states may make grace windows long; need fast incremental checkpoint design.
- Affinity model drift: how often to retrain or decay scoreboard to avoid stale mappings?

Implementation sketch (control plane + runtime):
- Control plane: lease broker service, affinity scorer service, token ledger service. Broker exposes lease API and emits audit events.
- Runtime: light-weight lease client integrated into local allocator; on reclaim receives preemption signal with lease_id and grace_window; runtime coordinates checkpoint and exposes reclaim progress API.

Acceptance criteria (for GA):
- End-to-end surge test: with 3x burst for 5 minutes across diverse model families, 95% of requests for premium tier maintain pre-burst latency within 20%.
- Billing: burst token accounting reconciles within 1 hour post-burst; no lost lease events.
- Operator tooling: console shows live leases and per-host affinity heatmap.

Appendix: short examples and notes:
- Example lease request: {tenant: "acme", requested_gpus: 2, duration: 120, affinity_hint: "prefer-rtx-a", burst: true}
- Preemption policy sketches: prefer reclaim of token-based leases first; prefer hosts with low affinity impact; avoid reclaim during ongoing canaries.
- Quick experiments to run in alpha: synthetic KV-heavy cold-starts vs warm hosts; token-decay parameter sweeps; cost model sensitivity to grace window length.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally pragmatic: focus on short leases and affinity routing rather than wholesale market changes. Looking for feedback on: affinity feature set, acceptable grace windows for enterprise SLAs, and how to scope burst token issuance rules.
